title: Seven in 10 people with diabetes do not know they have it
excerpt: Survey data show diabetes rising fastest in cities, and only about one in 20 people with it has the disease under control.
content:
About seven in 10 people with diabetes in Bangladesh do not know they have it, according to the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) 2022, The Daily Star reported on World Diabetes Day, Saturday, 14 November. The survey, run by the National Institute of Population Research and Training (NIPORT), covered 30,018 households.

Key figures from the survey

  • Unaware: 67% of women and 72% of men with diabetes, up from 59% and 61% in 2017-18.
  • Prevalence, aged 18 and over: 17% of women and 15% of men in 2022, up from 10% and 11% in 2017-18.
  • Under control: only 6% of women and 5% of men with diabetes knew they had it, were taking medicine and had their blood glucose controlled.
  • Cities: 24% of urban women and 21% of urban men had diabetes, against 14% and 13% in rural areas.
  • Wealth: 26% of women and 25% of men in the richest fifth of households, against 11% and 10% in the poorest.

Other estimates

Estimates differ by source and age group. The International Diabetes Federation (IDF) put the number of adults aged 20 to 79 with diabetes at about 1.39 crore (13.9 million) in 2024, and estimated that 39.1% of them were undiagnosed, The Business Standard reported. The Diabetic Association of Bangladesh (BADAS) said its registered patients rose from 30.61 lakh in 2014-15 to 69.37 lakh in 2024-25.

A study at Birdem General Hospital, cited by The Business Standard, found that 164 of 311 newly diagnosed type 2 patients (52.7%) already had at least one complication.

What officials said

Prof Prabath Chandra Biswas, director general of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), said every upazila health complex has a non-communicable disease (NCD) corner that gives diabetes and blood pressure medicine and routine checks, and that hospitals have been asked to use their own funds to avoid medicine shortages there, according to The Daily Star. Dr Md Nurul Islam of DGHS told The Business Standard that a national institute for metabolic and endocrine disease is planned and a site has been chosen.

Why it matters

Most people with diabetes find out only when complications appear, which pushes up costs for families and the health system. NGOs running community health, primary care and screening programmes can help close the gap, since free glucose and blood pressure tests are already offered at NCD corners but many people do not use them.

What to watch

Whether DGHS funds the planned expansion of NCD corners, and new national data from the next STEPS or BDHS survey.
